topic.title: Dinner after 8
topic.claim: The free office dinner after 8 isn't a perk; it's what your evening is worth to the company.
topic.moment: The food arrives at 8:15, the cab is free after 9, and somehow everyone is still at their desks at 9:30.

turn.believed: The company is looking after people who stay late.
turn.actually: A thali and a cab cost far less than the extra hours they keep you for.

topic.feeling: I got a free meal and lost my whole evening without noticing.
topic.villain: Perks timed to make late nights feel normal
topic.because: Once dinner is free, going home to cook feels like the silly choice. The perk sets the time everyone is expected to stay.
topic.payoff: Check what time the free food shows up. That's when they expect you to still be working.
topic.behaviour: Offices give out free meals and cabs only after a cut-off hour.
topic.group: Young professionals in metros who stay late at work
topic.send_to: The colleague who eats dinner at the office four nights a week
topic.why_now: Return-to-office pushes are bringing back the perks that keep you there longer.

score.why: The free office dinner is a perk that quietly sets the time you're expected to stay. It's a pure observation and an office take.

mechanism.broken_premise: None. The facts the post states are correct. Karnataka law does require employers who keep women at work between 8 PM and 6 AM to provide free transport, with security and GPS tracking. Swiggy's own 2026 release does say 25% of corporate employees at the offices it covers order food after 10 PM while still at the office. The rest of the post is interpretation: that the dinner's timing sets when people leave, and that a thali and cab cost less than the extra hours are worth. That is opinion and nothing in it is untrue. The one step it can't prove is that offices built their late nights on top of the cab rule, which is the writer's reading rather than a factual claim. Small caveats: the 'after 9' cab cut-off is an individual company's policy, not the law, which applies from 8 PM. The Swiggy figure measures late-night ordering in general, not late orders that come after a free office dinner.
mechanism.actual_mechanism: In Karnataka, Section 25 of the Shops and Commercial Establishments Act (amended in 2020) and the 2024 notification letting businesses stay open 24x7 allow women to work between 8 PM and 6 AM only with their written consent. The employer must also provide protection and free transport with security and GPS tracking, and post a notice about it at the main entrance. Office dinners and cab cut-off times are set by each company's own policy. The company pays for them, so the employee gets a meal and a ride, and the employer gets staff who are more likely to stay at their desks. Swiggy's 'Late Night Eats' service, launched in 2026, is based on its internal data showing that 25% of corporate employees at the 4,000+ offices it covers order food after 10 PM while still at work.

cover.headline: The free office dinner after 8 is [the price of your evening]
cover.sub: Look at what that thali actually buys the company.

paragraphs:
The free dinner after 8 isn't a perk. It's what your evening is worth to the company.
Swipe →
slides.why_swipe: How can free food be a bad deal?

paragraphs: The food arrives at 8:15. The cab is free after 9.
And somehow the whole floor is still at their desks at 9:30. Nobody asked anyone to stay.
slides.why_swipe: So why is everyone still there?

paragraphs: Someone says "khaana aa gaya, kha ke nikalte hain." You eat. Then a deck gets shared, and it's "bas ek call aur."
By then you're waiting for 9 anyway, because paying for an Uber when a free cab is minutes away feels silly.
slides.why_swipe: What does the company actually get out of it?

paragraphs: Now count what the dinner bought.
Those two hours were meant for the gym, a call home, or cooking your own dal.
You got a plate of food. The company got your evening.
slides.why_swipe: Why does it work on everyone?

paragraphs: Once dinner is free, going home to cook feels like the dumb choice.
So the perk picks your leaving time. You only think you did.
slides.why_swipe: Is the cab part of the trick too?

paragraphs: In fairness, the cab didn't begin as a trick. In Karnataka, if a company keeps women at work past 8 PM, the law says it must get them home. Free, and safe.
Fair rule. Offices just built their late nights on top of it.
slides.why_swipe: Does dinner at 8 at least end the day?

paragraphs: Dinner was supposed to get you to 9. Swiggy's own numbers say a quarter of people in the offices it delivers to are still ordering after 10. From work.
The biryani lands right as you reach for your bag. Odd timing.
slides.why_swipe: So how do you spot it in your own office?

paragraphs: Look at what time the free food shows up.
That's the hour they expect you to still be at your desk.

end.save: Read it again the next time you hear "kha ke nikalte hain" at 8:15.
end.send: Send to the colleague who eats dinner at the office four nights a week.

draft.alt_text: A text carousel arguing that free office dinners and cabs after a cut-off hour are not perks but a way for companies to keep employees' evenings. It walks through the 8:15 dinner and the free cab after 9, and the gym, call home or home-cooked dinner those hours were meant for. It argues the perk ends up deciding when people leave. It notes that in Karnataka, if a company keeps women at work past 8 PM, the law says it must get them home for free and safely, and that offices built their late nights on top of that rule. It cites Swiggy data that a quarter of people in the offices it delivers to are still ordering food after 10 PM from work. It ends by telling readers that the time the free food arrives is the time they are expected to still be at their desk.

Swiggy's own numbers say a quarter of people in the offices it delivers to are still ordering after 10. From work.

draft.caption:
The free office dinner doesn't feed you for working late. It's the reason you're still there at 9:30.

Khaana aa gaya, kha ke nikalte hain. Then the deck, then the call, then the free cab.

Once dinner is free, going home to cook your own dal starts to feel like the silly choice.

Send this to the colleague who eats dinner at the office four nights a week and still calls it a perk.
